name: Asenath
title: Joseph's Egyptian wife and mother of Ephraim and Manasseh
summary: Asenath belonged to the Egyptian ruling elite as the daughter of Potiphera, priest of the sun city On (Heliopolis). When Pharaoh elevated Joseph to the highest office in Egypt after he interpreted Pharaoh's dreams, Asenath was given to Joseph as a wife—an marital alliance that solidified Joseph's legitimacy within the Egyptian power structure. Before the seven years of famine began, Asenath bore the sons Manasseh and Ephraim. In a pivotal event toward the end of the patriarch Jacob's life, he chose to adopt these two grandsons as his own sons and blessed them with inheritance rights equal to his other sons (Gen 48). Asenath's children thus became ancestors of two of Israel's twelve tribes, and she herself secured a lasting place in Israel's salvation history. Her role in the narrative highlights how the biblical covenant story could unexpectedly include people from backgrounds outside Abraham's lineage.

keyEvents.title: Given to Joseph as a wife at his elevation
keyEvents.description: After Joseph interpreted Pharaoh's dreams and was elevated to rule over all Egypt, Pharaoh gave him Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, as a wife. The marriage marked Joseph's new position and gave him legitimacy in Egyptian society. Joseph was thirty years old when he entered service under Pharaoh.

keyEvents.title: The birth of Manasseh
keyEvents.description: Asenath bore Joseph's firstborn son Manasseh before the years of famine came. Joseph named him Manasseh, which can be linked to the Hebrew verb for 'to forget,' because God had made him forget all his hardship and his entire father's house.

keyEvents.title: The Birth of Ephraim
keyEvents.description: Asenath bore her second son Ephraim. Joseph named him Ephraim, which can be linked to the Hebrew word for 'fruitfulness,' because God had made him fruitful in the land where he had suffered.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in Jacob's Genealogy
keyEvents.description: Asenath is mentioned as the mother of Manasseh and Ephraim in the list of Jacob's family who came to Egypt, confirming her place in Israel's genealogy and her sons' belonging to the covenant people.

keyEvents.title: Jacob's Adoption and Blessing of Asenath's Sons
keyEvents.description: When Jacob was near death, he adopted Asenath's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, as his own and blessed them with inheritance rights equal to his other sons. Jacob placed the younger Ephraim before the firstborn Manasseh in the blessing—an expression that God's choice does not necessarily follow human conventions. Through this act, Asenath's sons were fully incorporated into Israel's tribal community.

versions.summary: Asenath was the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On (Heliopolis), and was given to Joseph as a wife by Pharaoh after Joseph interpreted Pharaoh's dreams. She became the mother of Joseph's two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, who later became ancestors of two of Israel's twelve tribes. Through this marriage, she became an important part of Israel's history, even though she herself was of Egyptian origin.
versions.title: Joseph's Egyptian Wife
versions.reason: [minor] The first two events ('Given to Joseph as wife' and 'Joseph's exaltation and marriage') overlap significantly—both refer to Gen 41:45-46 and concern the same marriage. It is recommended to merge them into a single event to avoid repetition.; [minor] The role 'matriarch' is somewhat imprecise for Asenath. She was not one of the classical matriarchs (Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Leah), but rather a wife and mother in the time of the patriarchs. Adding 'wife' or 'mother' as a role would provide a more complete picture.; [major] Footnotes are entirely missing. For a figure like Asenath, there are interesting historical, linguistic, and theological details that should be covered—for example, the meaning of her name, the city of On/Heliopolis, the pseudepigraphical work 'Joseph and Asenath', and the theological discussion about an Egyptian woman's place in Israel's family history.; [minor] The summary is good, but could mention that Jacob's adoption of Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen 48) gave her sons full tribal status in Israel—this further underscores her significance.

versions.summary: Asenath was the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On (Heliopolis), and was given to Joseph as wife by Pharaoh after Joseph interpreted Pharaoh's dreams and was elevated to second-in-command in Egypt. She became the mother of Joseph's two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, who were later adopted by Jacob as his own sons (Gen 48) and became ancestors of two of Israel's twelve tribes. Through this marriage and Jacob's adoption of her sons, Asenath became an important part of Israel's history, even though she herself was of Egyptian origin. Her role illustrates how God's plan for Israel included people from various nations.
versions.title: Joseph's Egyptian Wife
versions.reason: [minor] The summary closely resembles version 1 (starting identically with "Asenath was the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On (Heliopolis), and was given to Joseph as wife by Pharaoh..."). Since an earlier version exists with this wording, the text should be rephrased to offer a fresh perspective.; [minor] The role "matriarch" can be debated regarding Asenath. Traditionally, the matriarchs of Israel are considered to be Sarah, Rebekah, Leah, and Rachel. Asenath is the mother of two tribal founders but is not normally referred to as a "matriarch." A more precise designation could be "tribal mother" or another term that clarifies her contribution without confusing her with the four classical matriarchs.; [minor] The final event ("Jacob's blessing and adoption of Asenath's sons") primarily concerns Jacob and his actions, not directly Asenath. Nevertheless, it remains relevant to her profile, though the description could more clearly highlight its significance from Asenath's perspective.

versions.summary: Asenath came from the upper class of Egyptian society as the daughter of Potiphera, priest of the sun city On (Heliopolis). When Joseph was elevated to the highest official in Egypt after interpreting Pharaoh's dreams, Pharaoh gave him Asenath as a wife – a marriage that anchored Joseph's position within the Egyptian power elite. Together with Joseph she had sons Manasseh and Ephraim, both born before the seven years of famine occurred. At a decisive moment toward the end of the patriarch Jacob's life he adopted these two sons as his own and blessed them on equal footing with his other sons (Gen 48). Thus Asenath's children became ancestors of two of Israel's twelve tribes, and she herself became inseparably linked to Israel's salvation history. Her place in the story testifies that God's covenant and blessing could include people from all nations – a recurring theme in biblical revelation.
versions.title: Joseph's Egyptian wife and mother of Ephraim and Manasseh
versions.reason: [minor] The period c. 1900–1800 BC is somewhat early compared to many chronologies that place Joseph in Egypt closer to 1700–1600 BC (or possibly even later). Although there are various chronological frameworks, a broader or slightly adjusted timeframe would be more neutral.; [minor] Since this is version 3 and two earlier versions had similar introductions, the text should have sufficiently distinct wording. The current version has a clearly different approach focusing on the social class, but the final sentence stating that "God's covenant and blessing could include people from all nations" is a theological statement that goes somewhat beyond what the text explicitly says about Asenath herself. The Bible does not explicitly describe Asenath's faith or conversion, so this should be phrased more cautiously.; [minor] The blessing scene in Genesis 48 includes several important verses beyond those listed. Verses 13–20 contain the actual act of blessing and Jacob's crossing of his hands. It may be worth including some of these verses to provide a more complete picture.

footnotes.text: The name Asenath (Hebrew: אָסְנַת, 'Āsenath) is likely of Egyptian origin and may mean 'she who belongs to (the goddess) Neith' or 'belonging to Neith.' Neith was an ancient Egyptian goddess especially worshipped in Sais in Lower Egypt. The name is one of several Egyptian loanwords in the Books of Moses that confirm the story's Egyptian cultural context.

On (Hebrew: אוֹן) is identified with Heliopolis (Greek: 'City of the Sun'), one of ancient Egypt's foremost religious centers, located northeast of modern Cairo. The city was the main seat of sun worship for the god Ra, and its priesthood enjoyed very high social and political status throughout much of Egyptian history.

There is a pseudepigraphical work from about 100 BCE–100 CE known as "Joseph and Asenath", which expands on the story of Asenath's conversion from Egyptian idol worship to faith in the God of Israel before her marriage to Joseph. The text was popular in both Jewish and early Christian circles and offers a window into how later tradition understood intermarriage and conversion.

That Pharaoh gave Joseph a wife from the priesthood of Heliopolis fits well with Egyptian practice. Egyptian sources confirm that it was common for pharaohs to reward high-ranking servants through marriage to women from prominent families, which at the same time gave the recipient legitimacy and connection to the country's power elite.

Rabbinic tradition (Targum Pseudo-Jonathan and several midrashim) sometimes identifies Potiphera with Potiphar, Joseph's former master, although this is disputed among scholars. Other rabbinic sources regard Potiphera as a completely different person. The names are related in Hebrew but have different forms.

Jacob's adoption of Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen 48:5) is theologically significant because it fully incorporates Asenath's sons, of Egyptian maternal lineage, into Israel's covenant community. This can be seen as an early expression that God's plan of salvation includes people across ethnic boundaries—a theme repeated throughout the biblical narrative.

Archaeological findings from the Heliopolis area, including temple ruins and inscriptions, confirm the city's importance as a religious center in the second millennium BC. Although no direct archaeological traces of Asenath have been found, these discoveries support the historical framework surrounding the story of Joseph and his Egyptian connections.
